title: Lining sugar barrels at twelve
summary: He earned money lining barrels at a factory, with details of staves arriving by schooner.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: I was thinking once the other night, when you had been telling about those barrels, you never did work in the barrel factory. No, I used to line barrels.
You didn't work in the barrel factory. You didn't work in the barrel factory.
Yeah. You didn't work in the barrel factory.

Yeah. You see, the sugar barrels were made out of common staves. And they have a groove cut in for the head. Well, the sugar barrels, the staves were so thin that the groove was very shallow. So they had a lining. They put half way around on each side to reinforce the head, the grooves. And they used to give the kids, I don't know, I think so much, a hundred. Then they got fifty cents a hundred.
You did that work before you became a class, right?
Oh, yes. Yes. I was around about twelve years old.
And that factory was back on?
On St. Louis and Rushblade. Well, it ran from Rushblade to Taunty.
Was the canal, the Oak Basin, whatever it is there?

Well, it was there then. That's where all the staves used to come in by schooners, through that waterway. Well, I never got the staves out of here. All the lumber for the heads, the barrel heads. Now, all those oak staves. See the oak staves coming in? Yeah, the oak staves came by schooners too. The only thing that came by train was the sugar barrels. They'd get those staves already shaped. You just set up the barrels there and put the heads in them. But all the cypress, molasses barrels, and the whiskey barrels, they all made their wine barrels. They were made right there. They bought their raw lumber and shaped them, everything.
